prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at magic twist angles, founding moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is the clearest recent case in which band-structure theory preceded and directly guided a major experimental discovery. Bistritzer and MacDonald computed from a continuum electronic-structure model that flat bands appear near a magic twist angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group then found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle, and many laboratories have reproduced the phases. It created a tunable platform for correlated electrons, and the idea of using twist and stacking as a control knob has spread to many other materials. Five of my seven colleagues placed it in their top three and the theory-plus-experiment attribution is described in nearly the same terms by everyone, which is unusual for a candidate in this list. I ranked altermagnetism (B019) first because it is the cleanest conceptual advance in my own field of magnetism. After reading the openings, I weigh differently what can be defended in committee: no colleague ranked B019, so my high regard for it has not been tested against independent scientific scrutiny, whereas B017 has been examined from several angles and held up. I would still not drop B019 from the discussion, and it is my first alternative.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, sample-to-sample variation is large, and the full legacy may depend on later moire discoveries, so recognising it now could be called early. Attribution is also not fully clean: the 2018 experiments were carried out with Yuan Cao and Valla Fatemi, who are not in the supplied credit, and earlier theory on twisted bilayers (for example by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and by Suarez Morell and colleagues) bears on priority. A three-person prize necessarily omits other experimental groups such as Dean, Young and Kim, who established the hBN moire and later correlated phases.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a discovery in nature, and accepts B017 as high in originality while noting that the superconducting mechanism is not stable even if the central discovery is robust.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction he draws between the central discovery and the later phenomenology, and I would build the citation around the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated and superconducting states, not around a mechanism. On B029 I differ somewhat: I accept the new messenger window, but he himself finds the two-person allocation unsettled and the source associations only partly statistical. A prize whose credit is split among a very large collaboration seems to me harder to defend than one with a named prediction and a named experimental group.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B017 first as an experimentalist, valuing the controlled twist angle and the clear split between the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's discovery, while noting that Dean, Young and others are also part of the story.
responses.response: I share her reading of the attribution and her view that the timing is appropriate for the originating discovery. Where I qualify it: the credit gap is not only Dean and Young but also Cao and Fatemi, who did the 2018 measurements, and I would not describe the supplied trio as exhaustive. That is a limitation of the three-person rule, not a reason to prefer a candidate whose credit looks tidier only because the field is smaller. Her enthusiasm for B008 on interface control is well taken, but I agree with her own note that the real question there is whether the 1995 discovery or the MgO step carries the prize.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as the cleanest case of what can be measured, with a clear two-person credit, independent confirmation in many laboratories and timeliness that is arguably overdue.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing case and I take it seriously. Its attribution is cleaner than B017's, and the maturity is greater, and I cannot claim expertise in precision spectroscopy to dispute the physics. My reservation is about the margin: as Kroll's own opening and Johansson's both note, the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy lineage was recognised in 2005 and the single-ion clocks in 2012, so the committee must justify the lattice step as distinct. I therefore keep B041 as an alternative, not my first choice, and would be content to see it prevail if the committee judges the maturity advantage decisive.

responses.point: Johansson ranks topological insulators first on conceptual originality and maturity, but says leaving Mele out of a Kane-Molenkamp-Hasan trio is a real cost, and ranks B017 sixth as a little early but not unreasonable.
responses.response: I agree that B004 is conceptually excellent and I ranked it fourth myself, but his own remark on Mele shows why I do not put it first: the Kane-Mele theory, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, the HgTe observation and the 3D ARPES work make four overlapping contributions, so any three names is contestable, and the 2016 prize on topological phases lowers the margin. On his point that B017 is early, I partly agree, but I think the existence of the correlated phases, reproduced by many groups for eight years, is the thing that would be recognised, and that is not early.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and B017 third, describing the magic-angle prediction followed by decisive experiments as a satisfying prediction and confirmation, while observing that Cao and Fatemi may raise allocation questions.
responses.response: I agree that the prediction-confirmation structure is the strongest feature of B017, and he is right that the supplied credit does not address Cao and Fatemi. I would address this in the citation and in committee discussion, as the Academy has done before with experimental groups. On IceCube I accept his argument that the discovery changed an observational window, but his own acknowledgement that allocation among a large collaboration is the real difficulty, and that the TXS association rests on a modest chance-coincidence significance, leaves me unconvinced that it should come ahead of a prize with clean named credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the pairing mechanism and sample dependence in twisted bilayer graphene to be a matter of maturity or only of later phenomenology.
How to handle Cao, Fatemi and earlier twisted-bilayer theory in credit and citation when only three names can be chosen.

Whether altermagnetism (B019) is better understood and more robustly confirmed than my recollection suggests, since no colleague has tested it and my memory of the experimental timeline is unverified.
Whether the lattice-clock step is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes to override B017 on maturity and attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B017. For B019 and B008 my field (magnetism, electronic structure, spin dynamics) is close, which affects expertise but is not a personal or institutional connection that the profile documents.
